entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adam Reißner (c. 1494 – 1572) was a German humanist, mystic, hymn-writer, and poet, whose work bridged the late German Renaissance and the early Reformation era. Born in Mindelheim, Swabia, his intellectual journey took him from the vibrant academic centers of Ingolstadt and Heidelberg to a period of military service under Georg von Frundsberg, eventually settling into a life of scholarly pursuit and religious contemplation. His significance lies in his unique synthesis of classical erudition with profound spiritual introspection, contributing to both secular literature and Protestant hymnody during a period of intense religious and cultural upheaval in Central Europe.

Reißner's early career saw him as a student at the University of Ingolstadt (1512) and later at Heidelberg, where he studied under the famed humanist Jakob Wimpfeling. A pivotal, albeit unusual, chapter of his life involved serving as secretary to the "Father of the Landsknechte," Georg von Frundsberg, during the Italian Wars, including the infamous Sack of Rome in 1527. This firsthand experience of military conflict and human suffering deeply impacted his worldview. Upon returning to Mindelheim around 1530, he devoted himself to writing, producing notable works such as the epic poem *Historia Fronspergii* (1537), a biographical account of Frundsberg, and numerous hymns, many of which found their way into Protestant hymnals. His most enduring contribution, perhaps, is his adaptation of the *Teutsche Theologey* (1528) from the anonymous *Theologia Germanica*, a mystical text that influenced Martin Luther.

entities.summary:
Adam Reißner (also spelled Reusner or Reissner), born in Mindelheim around 1500, emerged as a prominent German mystic, hymn-writer, and poet during the tumultuous Early Modern period, profoundly shaping the spiritual and literary landscape of the Protestant Reformation. His life, spanning from 1500 to 1572, placed him at the heart of intellectual and religious ferment in Western Europe, where he navigated the seismic shifts of theological debate and the burgeoning print culture, becoming a significant voice in the development of vernacular sacred song. Reißner is particularly remembered for his contributions to German hymnody, which provided accessible spiritual comfort and theological instruction to the common people in an era of profound religious change.

Educated at the universities of Ingolstadt and Heidelberg, Reißner initially pursued a path in humanistic studies before embracing the burgeoning Protestant movement, albeit with a distinct mystical bent. His most enduring literary achievement is the collection of hymns, many of which were first published in the widely influential Strasbourg hymnals of the mid-16th century. Notably, his hymn "Ich armer Mensch, ich armer Sünder" ("I, poor man, I, poor sinner") became a staple of Protestant worship, embodying the era's focus on personal penitence and divine grace. Beyond hymns, Reißner penned theological treatises and mystical writings, often reflecting a deep, introspective piety that resonated with both Lutheran and Anabaptist circles, bridging different Protestant currents through shared spiritual experience.
